title: Canada, Elementary and Secondary
subject: other-countries
year_note: Canadian elementary and secondary content, roughly ages 8 to 14. The NZ year band is a rough equivalent by age, not a curriculum match.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Canada?
questions.explanation: Ottawa, in the province of Ontario, is Canada's capital, even though Toronto is the country's biggest city.

questions.prompt: Toronto, Canada's biggest city, is in which province?
questions.explanation: Toronto is the capital of Ontario and Canada's most populated city.

questions.prompt: Montreal is the biggest city in which province?
questions.explanation: Montreal is Quebec's biggest city, though Quebec City, not Montreal, is the provincial capital.

questions.prompt: Vancouver sits on which coast of Canada?
questions.explanation: Vancouver is on Canada's west coast, on the Pacific Ocean.

questions.prompt: How many provinces make up Canada?
questions.explanation: Canada has ten provinces, plus three territories in the north.

questions.prompt: Besides its ten provinces, how many territories does Canada have in the north?
questions.explanation: The three northern territories are Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of British Columbia?
questions.explanation: Victoria, on Vancouver Island, is the capital of British Columbia, though Vancouver is the province's biggest city.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Alberta?
questions.explanation: Edmonton is Alberta's capital, while Calgary is the province's largest city.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Manitoba?
questions.explanation: Winnipeg is Manitoba's capital and by far its biggest city.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Saskatchewan?
questions.explanation: Regina is Saskatchewan's capital, though Saskatoon is the province's biggest city.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Nova Scotia?
questions.explanation: Halifax, on the Atlantic coast, is Nova Scotia's capital and biggest city.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of New Brunswick?
questions.explanation: Fredericton is New Brunswick's capital, even though Saint John and Moncton are both bigger cities.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Prince Edward Island?
questions.explanation: Charlottetown is the capital of Prince Edward Island, Canada's smallest province.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Newfoundland and Labrador?
questions.explanation: St. John's, on the island of Newfoundland, is the capital of Newfoundland and Labrador.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Nunavut, Canada's newest and most northern territory?
questions.explanation: Iqaluit is the capital of Nunavut, a territory created in 1999 for Canada's Inuit.

questions.prompt: Which mountain range runs through western Canada?
questions.explanation: The Rocky Mountains stretch through British Columbia and Alberta.

questions.prompt: The Canadian Shield, which covers much of central and northern Canada, is best described as which of these?
choices: A huge region of ancient, rocky land
A mountain range in the west
questions.explanation: The Canadian Shield is an enormous area of very old rock, shaped by ancient glaciers, covering much of Ontario, Quebec and the north.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the five Great Lakes?
questions.explanation: The five Great Lakes are Superior, Huron, Michigan, Erie and Ontario. Lake Winnipeg is a different, separate lake in Manitoba.

questions.prompt: Canada shares the Great Lakes with which country?
questions.explanation: The Great Lakes sit on the border between Canada and the United States.

questions.prompt: Which river carries water from the Great Lakes out to the Atlantic Ocean?
questions.explanation: The St. Lawrence River flows from the Great Lakes, past Montreal and Quebec City, out to the Atlantic.

questions.prompt: Which river is the longest in Canada?
questions.explanation: The Mackenzie River flows through the Northwest Territories to the Arctic Ocean and is Canada's longest river.

questions.prompt: Which bay, between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, has the highest tides in the world?
questions.explanation: The Bay of Fundy's tides can rise and fall by more than 15 metres, the biggest tidal range on Earth.

questions.prompt: Which three oceans touch Canada's coastline?
questions.explanation: Canada touches the Atlantic Ocean in the east, the Pacific in the west and the Arctic in the north, giving it the longest coastline of any country.

questions.prompt: Indigenous peoples had been living in what is now Canada for roughly how long before Europeans arrived?
questions.explanation: Indigenous peoples have lived across what is now Canada for thousands of years before any European set foot there.

questions.prompt: The Inuit traditionally live in which part of Canada?
questions.explanation: The Inuit are Indigenous people of the Arctic, traditionally living across Canada's far north.

questions.prompt: The Métis, one of Canada's three recognised Indigenous peoples, are a distinct people descended from whom?
choices: First Nations and European fur traders
questions.explanation: The Métis Nation grew from families with both First Nations and European, mostly French, fur-trade ancestry, and developed its own distinct culture.

questions.prompt: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy, a long-standing alliance of Indigenous nations in what is now Ontario and New York, is also known by which name?
questions.explanation: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy is also called the Six Nations, after the six member nations it eventually included.

questions.prompt: European fur traders who paddled canoes over long distances between trading posts were known as what?
questions.explanation: Voyageurs were the fur traders, mostly French Canadian, who paddled and portaged canoes loaded with furs and goods across the country.

questions.prompt: New France, Canada's first major European colony, was settled mainly by people from which country?
questions.explanation: New France was France's colony along the St. Lawrence River, centred on Quebec City, founded in the early 1600s.

questions.prompt: The 1759 Battle of the Plains of Abraham, a turning point in the fight for control of Canada, was fought near which city?
questions.explanation: The battle was fought on high ground just outside the walls of Quebec City, between British and French forces.

questions.prompt: Canadian Confederation, when Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick joined together as one country, happened in which year?
questions.explanation: Confederation took place on 1 July 1867, a date still celebrated every year as Canada Day.

questions.prompt: Who was Canada's first Prime Minister?
questions.explanation: John A. Macdonald became Canada's first Prime Minister when Confederation took place in 1867.

questions.prompt: Which of these provinces did NOT join Canada at Confederation in 1867?
questions.explanation: Only Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick joined in 1867. Manitoba became a province in 1870, and other provinces joined later still.

questions.prompt: The Canadian Pacific Railway, completed in 1885, is famous for doing what?
choices: Linking the country from coast to coast
Connecting Canada to the United States only
questions.explanation: The Canadian Pacific Railway joined British Columbia to the rest of Canada, fulfilling a promise made when BC joined Confederation.

questions.prompt: Which First World War battle, fought in 1917, is often seen as a defining moment for Canada as a nation?
questions.explanation: At Vimy Ridge in April 1917, Canadian troops fighting together as one force captured ground that other Allied armies had not been able to take.

questions.prompt: The Battle of Vimy Ridge was fought in which country?
questions.explanation: Vimy Ridge is in northern France, where the battle was fought in April 1917.

questions.prompt: On D-Day in June 1944, Canadian troops landed on which beach in Normandy?
questions.explanation: Juno Beach was the section of the Normandy coast where Canadian forces landed on D-Day, 6 June 1944.

questions.prompt: The Statute of Westminster, passed in 1931, did what for Canada?
choices: Gave Canada full power to make its own laws, separate from Britain
Ended Canada's ties to the Commonwealth
questions.explanation: The Statute of Westminster in 1931 gave Canada and other dominions full legislative independence from the British Parliament.

questions.prompt: Canada's Constitution was fully brought under Canadian control, without needing approval from Britain, in which year?
questions.explanation: In 1982, the Constitution was patriated, meaning Canada no longer needed the British Parliament's approval to change it.

questions.prompt: What document, added when the Constitution was patriated in 1982, guarantees Canadians' basic rights and freedoms?
choices: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
questions.explanation: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms became part of the Constitution in 1982 and protects rights such as free speech and equality before the law.

questions.prompt: What kind of government does Canada have?
choices: A direct democracy with no parliament
questions.explanation: Canada is a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy: laws are made by an elected parliament.

questions.prompt: Who leads Canada's government day to day?
questions.explanation: The Prime Minister leads the government and is normally the head of the political party with the most seats in Parliament.

questions.prompt: Canada's Parliament is made up of two houses. What are they called?
choices: The House of Commons and the Senate
The House of Lords and the Commons
questions.explanation: Members of the House of Commons are elected, while members of the Senate are appointed.

questions.prompt: Who officially represents the King in Canada?
questions.explanation: The Governor General carries out the King's formal, ceremonial duties in Canada, since Canada is a constitutional monarchy.

questions.prompt: Which of these areas is mainly run by Canada's provinces, rather than the federal government?
questions.explanation: Under Canada's constitution, provinces run their own schools and hospitals, while the federal government handles things like defence and money.

questions.prompt: What are Canada's two official languages?
questions.explanation: Canada has been officially bilingual, in English and French, since 1969.

questions.prompt: In which province is French the majority language?
questions.explanation: Quebec is home to most of Canada's French speakers, and French is the province's sole official language.

questions.prompt: Which is Canada's only officially bilingual province, with both English and French as official languages by law?
questions.explanation: New Brunswick is Canada's only province that is legally bilingual, alongside sizeable French and English speaking communities.

questions.prompt: Canada's national flag, adopted in 1965, features which symbol?
questions.explanation: The red and white maple leaf flag was adopted in 1965, replacing an earlier flag that included the British Union Jack.

questions.prompt: Which animal is a well known symbol of Canada, and appears on the five cent coin?
questions.explanation: The beaver has been a symbol of Canada since the fur trade days and appears on the nickel, Canada's five cent coin.

questions.prompt: What is the name of Canada's national anthem?
questions.explanation: O Canada became Canada's official national anthem in 1980, though it had been sung since the 1880s.

questions.prompt: Canada Day, marking Confederation in 1867, is celebrated on what date?
questions.explanation: Canada Day falls on 1 July every year, the date Confederation took effect in 1867.

questions.prompt: What is Canada's federal police force commonly called?
choices: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police, or Mounties
questions.explanation: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police, nicknamed the Mounties, is Canada's national police force, known for its red uniform.

questions.prompt: What colours appear on the Canadian flag?
questions.explanation: The Canadian flag is red and white, the colours officially declared Canada's national colours in 1921.

questions.prompt: Insulin, used to treat which disease, was discovered by Frederick Banting and Charles Best at the University of Toronto?
questions.explanation: Banting and Best discovered insulin in 1921 and 1922, giving people with diabetes a life saving treatment.

questions.prompt: The first practical implantable cardiac pacemaker was built in the 1950s by which Canadian engineer?
questions.explanation: John Hopps, an engineer working in Ottawa, built the first practical pacemaker in 1950, though it took years more work before implantable versions were used in patients.

questions.prompt: The idea of dividing the world into standard time zones was proposed by which Canadian?
questions.explanation: Sandford Fleming, a Scottish born Canadian engineer, proposed worldwide standard time in the 1870s and 1880s, the system still used today.

questions.prompt: Standard time divides the world up into what?
questions.explanation: Standard time splits the globe into time zones, each keeping a set time rather than every town using its own local sun time.

questions.prompt: The sport of basketball was invented by James Naismith, who was born in which country?
questions.explanation: James Naismith was born in Ontario, Canada, and invented basketball in 1891 while working in the United States.

questions.prompt: Alexander Graham Bell did key early work developing the telephone at his family's home in which Canadian town?
questions.explanation: Bell's family home in Brantford, Ontario, is where he did important early experiments on the telephone, before patenting it in the United States.
